## Design

### 2026-10-28: Day 1: Start

**3h**

Day 1: Start

For this week, I am creating a machine that lets you play the old game Tetris on it. I personally love Tetris,  and playing it on my school Chromebook on this one sketchy Russian unblocked site was a canon event for all of my friends back at my old school.

For this week, I have also challenged myself by not using Gemini at all, whether it is for simple information gleaning or deep questioning. I am pretty anxious about this, but we'll see how it goes.

So, to start with, I decided what my project would do, and how it would accomplish its tasks. When I first thought of Tetris, I thought of those old-school arcade-style things that would house the game, so I am going to try to emulate it based on that.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/08f086caa9694711a421772f4c4b571b0b899aec72e6573661133cc153e7b4a3.png)
(Obviously not that big, but you get the idea)

Furthermore, I would need a screen and controls to move the blocks around. For my week 2 project, I used a joystick module (the KY-023), and I thought that module might also work here as a joystick to move the blocks. I also need to have 1 button to start and stop the game, 1 to pause, and 1 for block storage. In Tetris, if you don't want to use a block at the moment, you can put it in, like, a 1-block inventory, and swap it out later.

I decided to start looking for good products. For my display, I originally wanted to use an OLED screen to make some snazzy animations of the blocks, but then realized the cost of those things. To put it in perspective, a regular Tetris map is around a 10x20 board. The OLED screen I am using for my week 2 project is a 1.63" board, and it costs $3.  1.63" is a diagonal, so the height is ~0.6 and the length ~1. That means they have to fit 20 Tetris squares in 1", or 1 Tetris square per 0.05 in. At that point, a person cannot even see the blocks! Furthermore, a larger screen costs much more money, which I cannot afford because I am committed to a Tier 1 plan.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/3037ddb18efa1df8d215b694eb49c8c63b2ea916bfe4d2b6a4f59d4ef7904224.png)
(I know it says a dollar, but that is the New Shopper promo, which I am 99% sure that Hack Club does not qualify for)

For inspiration, I decided to look at the guide. There, I learned about LED matrices. LED matrices are perfect because only 1 object is falling at once, so it doesn't look too cluttered, and they are extremely cheap. I managed to find a great deal, with 4 connected 8x8s stacked together. This is genuinely perfect because original Tetris is on a 10x20, and this is on an 8x32. Not too far off, and the extra height can be used for some extra graphics.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/ff4499d69d9f3d40f0f35adbb8d544fec76d69855379034b27a240ddaabbaac6.png)
(I was pretty worried that it would be confusing because you can only see 1 color, red, but I think it doesn't matter too much because there is only 1 piece falling, and the mess at the bottom can be seen as 1 big spiky blob without any real gameplay changes)

Next, I needed a good joystick module, as well as some buttons. This did not take too long, because I just needed to find a KY-023 (which I already stated I wanted) as well as a few 12 mm buttons. I considered using the 6 mm buttons I have at home, but I really feel like that will be way too uncomfortable for the player to use.

I found this pretty cheap joystick module:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/3717c250f31c571c6c9611b56f657a3ec946dd7be0dc9199b681469d3cd3393c.png)

And this set of 12 mm buttons:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/29ac01d5db514c07bf657bc4f639eadde7136e21ab65d8c2a9b73687fe8aff5f.png)
(I was really happy with this set because even though it cost significantly more than the others, it was multicolor, so it would be really easy for the user to distinguish between the different buttons and actions after a playthrough)

After finalizing all of my parts, I went on to work on my schematic. The thing is, I don't really know how to use KiCad. For my PCB week, I used EasyEDA, but then had a whole mess because, for some reason, the system was not accepting the JSON files from EasyEDA, so I had to transfer the files into KiCad and submit like that, and last week, I just followed what Gemini said, so in actuality, I have no idea what I am doing.

I watched a few beginner tutorials on KiCad, and this one made by the DigiKey company was especially useful. I  am not sure, but I think KiCad and DigiKey are working together, so they had a really comprehensive guide. (https://www.digikey.com/en/maker/projects/beginners-guide-to-kicad/eb0ae92f5dae49e489f02c10f3edfc60)

Then I needed to start entering my parts. Just like last week, I am using my Raspberry Pi, so I have to use the Raspberry Pi HAT library. I imported the file in no problem, but then I had to study up on the pin connections again. See, last week as well, I learned the pin connections, but I didn't really have experience working with the GPIO pins and what they do. After a while, I decided to prolong it (like usual), and start working on my components. I went to add to get my LED matrix, before coming to realize that they don't have the model I am using.

This made me have to rewatch the video on creating new components from DigiKey again. The explanation was good, but I was half asleep and couldn't understand anything, so I had to watch it a few times before anything sank in.

After this, I created my part, started wiring, and that is where I ended off today.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/e9d31f252aafca108d07faa3e6b4e45de771597c61f1e3d0b4eea4613af3df17.png)

### 2026-10-31: Day 2: Schematic & voltage

**3h**

Day 2: Schematic & voltage

Today I worked on my schematic and worked on my voltage calculations and decided whether my system needed any resistors and capacitors.

Beginning with the schematic, I worked on the remaining parts. This was pretty tricky, because I am really used to EasyEDA, and the different keys and (personally) horrible shortcuts menu were absolutely annoying. I had to make a few new parts today.

Starting out, I made the parts for buttons. The buttons work with a simple push, or something like this:

![Screenshot 2026-10-31 132436](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/49ff609e40159cfebaa9a444881203d987dd54289077a37da8244da88344bde4.png)

This shows that when the button is pushed down, the connections allow the current to flow through. I originally tried to make my thing as refined as this, but then just gave up. The reason being, I am not going to make a PCB; I am just going to get the schematic so I know how to connect everything when I get my parts. I made it just like a box and kept 4 protrusions to allow for connections. If you notice the schematic symbol, you only need to connect to 2 of the 4 because 2 of them are already connected in a line anyway. I came up with this as my button:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/7b3bce2d9cc6187f778708a587f0b7c58abe116b5054d38609298cea7ce55d9e.png)

Once that was done, I had to make the joystick. The joystick is a KY-023. It was relatively simple to make because I have experience working with it from the robotic arm project. What I did was make it with 5 pins: GND, VCC, VRX, VRY, and SW. Confession: I did not know that the joysticks came with a built-in switch, so that means I could have gotten 1 less button. This doesn't affect me, though, because for the cost, it is cheaper to buy 10 than a single 1.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/c664bad694b00553049fd343163c660e08b4290a5af1fbc84bbaf721eb3cd3b1.png)

Then I needed to start studying up on my connections. I didn't know the power requirements for these different components or the specialized terminology.

I started with the power connections. For the KY-023, it requires a maximum of 5V and a minimum of 3.3V. Thankfully, the Arduino board did have a port for 3.3V, so I plugged it into that. It took me a while to find, but I eventually found the datasheet to confirm this.

https://www.alldatasheet.com/datasheet-pdf/pdf/2134620/JOY-IT/KY-023-JOY-IT.html

Next, I went on to the LED Matrix. This took a lot of time, actually, because I needed to find the correct one. The one listed in the product description said MAX7129, but this data sheet was pretty difficult to find. Eventually, I managed to find one and looked at the information. That is when I realized an important part: I was using the 4x1 matrix, and they just had 1 module:

![Screenshot 2026-10-31 142149](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/0208bbcc20a442f9d966af1f56755de56804cd5d956cc66227de0a3028df5622.png)
(mine

![Screenshot 2026-10-31 142200](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/29891d63dacfb1f12f59725af33b8ef7818f5f6ba7cd78e502de9e44c9c66229.png)
)
(theirs)

I had to look into something called "daisy-chaining". Daisy-chaining refers to when you connect the output pins of one object to the input pins of another and rinse and repeat. If you look closely. you can see that the modules in both are the same, but the boards are more in number. This shows that the voltage needs to be high, but not significantly higher than before. I chose to use 5V for this.

Now the kind of embarrassing section. So I might just be a bit dumb, but I thought that we were supposed to connect the button to power too, because I thought that stopping the game would have to pull the power. This was a very wrong assumption. I spent like 30 min scrambling around trying to find how to connect the buttons to power before I finally realized that it would just need to be connected to GPIO pins and work through the code. Splendid.

After this, I worked on GPIO pins. This time, I started with buttons. For this, I needed to learn all of the Arduino pins special uses. This was much easier than learning the Raspberry Pi because the Raspberry Pi gives absolutely no labeling; the pins are close together, and online models kind of suck for it. The Arduino is much more self-explanatory.

I found a few sources helping explain the difference between analog and digital pins. That was really the only confusion I had, but after I got it, it was pretty self-explanatory, with the VRX and VRY going to analog, and everything else to digital.

I just routed everything together. Fun.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/879a6bbf7c135fed6f7cd1a9be06d00ff745b30aeab4bd43a0d18131c0d71be7.png)

Finally, I worked on the resistor calculations. I thought that nothing really needed a resistor, because whenI used to play with my LEDS, they would need a resistor, but nothing else. I watched a few videos on how to tell if you needed one, and the best explanation was to do it yourself. I did the calculations, but figuring everything out was actually kind of hard, ngl. It took me like an hour and a half to understand everything, but these are my finished calculations and notes.

![Screenshot 2026-10-31 144319](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/2d94da39cda7bbb211fc6c8d676464c17ebb420cbbcf0f8d6db4ec453142529a.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-31 144325](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/5140ae7810687b4e6b83319a80e11852d4443638892a8896beb73242b09580ac.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-31 144329](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/37a4ab6bb489022f3750af2117f21840081e0e1b2c49f89125b903036d67c97e.png)

Oh, and the reason I started working on the resistor was because iI relaied an LED matrix, is just a bunch of LEDS, which love to suck up voltage and kill themselves.

That is all I accomplished today!
